topics.title: Tú or usted? How formal to be in Spain
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about how people address each other in Spain. This is habit, not law: it varies by region, age, workplace and person, so listen to how others speak.
topics.intro: Spanish has two words for you when you speak to one person: tú and usted. Tú is the usual choice with friends, family, colleagues and young people, and usted shows respect to older strangers or in formal situations.
topics.question: ¿Hay una forma formal de decir you en tu idioma? (Does your language have a formal way to say you?)
facts: Use tú with friends, family, children and people of your own age.
Use usted with older people you do not know, and when you want to show respect.
The verb changes: with tú you say ¿Cómo estás? and with usted you say ¿Cómo está?
In many workplaces colleagues use tú, even with the boss. Listen to what the others say.
With a group of friends in Spain, say vosotros. Use ustedes for a formal group. In Latin America, ustedes is used for every group.
Not sure? Start with usted and wait. Often the other person says: Puedes tutearme (You can use tú with me).

topics.title: Greetings: dos besos, handshake, ¡Buenas!
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about greetings in Spain. This is habit, not law: it varies by region, age, situation and person. Follow what the other person does.
topics.intro: In Spain people greet with a word first, and often with a touch: dos besos (two kisses on the cheeks) or a handshake. What is usual depends on the region, the age and the situation.
topics.question: ¿Cómo saludas en tu país? (How do you greet people in your country?)
facts: Dos besos: you touch cheeks, one side and then the other, and the kiss is mostly in the air. It is common between two women and between a woman and a man who know each other.
Between men, a handshake is most common. Relatives and close friends may hug or kiss.
At a first meeting in a formal or work situation, a handshake is safe. If the other person leans in for dos besos, go along.
Say ¡Buenos días! until lunchtime, ¡Buenas tardes! from lunchtime until it gets dark, and ¡Buenas noches! in the evening and at night.
¡Buenas! is a short, friendly greeting for any time of day. Many people say it when they enter a shop, a bar, a lift or a waiting room.
Customs differ: some places use one kiss, and some people prefer no contact. A handshake is always fine.

topics.question: ¿A qué hora comes en tu país? (What time do you eat lunch in your country?)
facts: Many people have desayuno (breakfast) between 7 and 9 am, comida (lunch) between 2 and 4 pm and cena (dinner) between 9 and 10 pm.

On Sundays many shops are closed. Each community sets its own rules, and tourist areas (zonas de gran afluencia turística) can open more often.
A festivo (public holiday) is like a Sunday: most shops, banks and offices are closed. A farmacia de guardia stays open for emergencies.
Banks and public offices are usually open in the morning, Monday to Friday. For many offices you need a cita previa.
Look for the word horario on the door or check the shop online. Hours differ by town, season and shop.

topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about bars and restaurants in Spain, as of 2026. Tipping and paying habits are custom, not law, and differ by place. Menu prices normally include IVA (VAT) and service.
topics.intro: In a Spanish bar you usually pay at the end, you ask for la cuenta (the bill), and a tip is a small extra, not a rule. Friends often take turns paying for a round.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se paga en un bar en tu país? (How do you pay in a bar in your country?)
facts: Ask for the bill with: La cuenta, por favor. At a table you usually pay at the end. At the counter, many bars ask you to pay when you leave. If you are not sure, ask: ¿Pago ahora o luego?
Service and IVA (VAT) are included in the prices. A propina (tip) is not required.
Many people leave a few coins for good service, or round up the bill. It is a small thank you.
Invitar means to pay for others. Friends often pay a ronda (a round of drinks) in turns: Esta ronda la pago yo.
To split the bill, say: Pagamos a medias (half each). Small bars cannot always make separate bills, so ask first.
Most places take cards and contactless, but some small bars prefer cash for small amounts. Ask: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?

topics.question: ¿Qué comes normalmente al mediodía? (What do you usually eat at midday?)

Tapas are small portions to share with a drink. A ración is larger, and a media ración is half of it. In some cities, such as Granada, a free tapa often comes with the drink.
Cena (dinner) often starts around 9 pm and is usually lighter than comida. A merienda is an afternoon snack, especially for children.
Every region has typical dishes, for example paella in the Comunitat Valenciana, gazpacho in Andalucía, fabada in Asturias and pulpo a la gallega in Galicia.

The Fallas in València take place in March and end on the night of 19 March, when the large figures are burned.
The Sanfermines in Pamplona run from 6 to 14 July. The encierro (bull run) takes place in the morning.
The Feria de Abril in Sevilla is held in spring, after Semana Santa. Your own town has fiestas patronales too: the programme is on the town hall website.

topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about household waste in Spain, as of 2026. topics.intro: In Spain you sort your rubbish into coloured containers, and the colours are the same in most towns, but not in all. Ask your town hall if something looks different.
topics.question: ¿Cómo separas la basura en tu país? (How do you sort rubbish in your country?)
facts: Yellow container (contenedor amarillo): packaging (envases) made of plastic, cans and cartons.
Blue container (contenedor azul): paper and cardboard. Flatten boxes first.
Green container (contenedor verde, often called iglú): glass bottles and jars. Take off the lids. Ceramics, mirrors and drinking glasses do not go in.
Brown container (contenedor marrón): organic waste, such as food scraps. The law requires separate collection, but how it works depends on your town.
Everything else (resto) goes into another container, usually grey, green or black, depending on your town. Some towns use a key card or fixed hours.
Furniture, batteries, electronics, oil and chemicals go to the punto limpio (recycling centre). Many towns also collect old furniture: ask your town hall.

facts: You often need a cita previa for the Seguridad Social, Extranjería (the immigration office), the SEPE (the employment office), the town hall, the Agencia Tributaria (tax office), the DGT (driving licence) and the centro de salud.
Book on the official website of the office, or by phone. The appointment itself is free. Be careful with websites that sell appointments: they are not official.
You may need your passport or NIE (foreigner's identity number), an email address and a phone number. Some websites ask for a digital certificate or Cl@ve.
If there are no free appointments, try again later, on another day, or at another office of the same type.
On the day, arrive ten minutes early with the justificante (confirmation) and all your papers. A missed appointment is usually lost.
If you cannot come, cancel (anular) or change (cambiar) the appointment, so that someone else can use it.

topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on the Ley de Bases de Régimen Local (Ley 7/1985) and information from town halls. Required documents and online options differ by municipality, so check your ayuntamiento's page (as of 2026).
topics.intro: Everyone who lives in Spain should be registered in the padrón municipal, the list of residents kept by the town hall (ayuntamiento). The proof is the certificado de empadronamiento, and you will be asked for it surprisingly often.
topics.question: ¿Tienes que registrar tu dirección en tu país? (Do you have to register your address in your home country?)
facts: Under the Ley de Bases de Régimen Local, every person who lives in a municipality has to be registered in its padrón. It is called empadronarse.
The rule applies to everybody who lives there, whatever their legal status. Registering is not the same as having a residence permit.
You register at the ayuntamiento of the place where you live, usually after you have a place to stay. Many town halls ask for an appointment (cita previa).
Documents vary by town hall. Usually you show your passport or identity document and a contract, deed or other proof that you live at the address, and sometimes the owner's permission.
The certificado de empadronamiento proves where you live. It is often needed for the tarjeta sanitaria, school places, foreigner paperwork and some local services.
If you move within Spain, register at the new address. Some residents must also renew the registration regularly, so ask your town hall about your case.

topics.title: Public health: tarjeta sanitaria, centro de salud, urgencias
topics.sourceNote: General orientation from the Ministerio de Sanidad, the Seguridad Social and Real Decreto-ley 7/2018 on universal access (boe.es). Health care is run by each comunidad autónoma, so the details differ by region. Access depends on your situation; ask at your centro de salud (as of 2026).
topics.intro: Spain has a public health system, the Sistema Nacional de Salud, run by the regions, and you reach it through the tarjeta sanitaria. Whether you can get the card depends on your situation, so it is worth asking early.
topics.question: ¿Cómo funciona el médico en tu país? (How does going to the doctor work in your country?)
facts: Access to public health care is not automatic for everybody. It depends on things such as working and paying contributions, residence and your personal situation. Under a 2018 law, people who live in Spain without a residence permit can also have a right to care, with conditions and steps that depend on the region.
Workers and their families are usually covered through the Seguridad Social. The INSS (Instituto Nacional de la Seguridad Social) can confirm your right to care.
The tarjeta sanitaria is issued by your comunidad autónoma. It assigns you a centro de salud, a médico de cabecera (family doctor) and a nurse.
For a normal problem you go to the centro de salud, usually by making an appointment (cita previa). The family doctor can send you to a specialist.
In an emergency call 112, the European emergency number. Hospital urgencias (emergency rooms) treat serious cases, and emergency care is not refused.
The doctor gives you a receta (prescription), often electronic, and you collect the medicine at a farmacia. The amount you pay depends on your situation.

topics.intro: Most home rentals in Spain are governed by the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (LAU), which sets minimum tenant rights. Your contract (contrato de alquiler) adds the details, so read it before you sign.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se alquila una vivienda en tu país? (How do people rent a home in your country?)
facts: The landlord (arrendador or casero) usually asks for a fianza (deposit) of one month's rent for housing. It is often paid into a regional deposit office.
On top of the fianza, a landlord can ask for an extra guarantee, but the law limits it. Check the current limit in the LAU.
The parties agree the length of the contract. If it is shorter than five years, it is extended year by year up to five (seven if the landlord is a company), unless the tenant gives notice.
A tenant can usually leave after the first six months by giving the landlord 30 days' notice. The contract may add conditions, so read that clause.
Since 2023 the LAU says that estate agency and contract costs are paid by the landlord. Ask who pays what before you sign.
Water, electricity, gas and internet are often separate bills. The comunidad de propietarios fee for shared costs may be paid by the owner or passed to you, depending on the contract.

topics.title: The school system: infantil, primaria, ESO, bachillerato, FP
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on the Ministerio de Educación, Formación Profesional y Deportes. Schools are run by the comunidades autónomas, so enrolment dates, subjects and languages of teaching differ (as of 2026).
topics.intro: School in Spain is compulsory from the age of 6 to 16, and it is organised in stages: infantil, primaria, ESO and then bachillerato or formación profesional. Each comunidad autónoma runs its own schools and enrolment.
topics.question: ¿A qué edad empieza el colegio en tu país? (At what age does school start in your country?)
facts: Educación infantil is for ages 0 to 6, in two cycles. It is not compulsory, and the second cycle (3 to 6) is offered free in public schools.
Educación primaria lasts six years, from ages 6 to 12, and it is compulsory.
ESO, Educación Secundaria Obligatoria, lasts four years, from 12 to 16. At the end students can get the título de Graduado en ESO.
Education is compulsory from 6 to 16. After ESO, students can continue in bachillerato (two years, ages 16 to 18) or in formación profesional (FP).
FP is vocational training. It has levels, from basic to higher, and some give access to university.
There are public, concertados (private, partly publicly funded) and private schools. Enrolment (matrícula) and school places follow rules set by each region, so ask the regional education office.

topics.intro: To look for work in Spain you can use the public employment service, your comunidad's office, job websites and personal contacts. First check that your permit allows you to work, and then learn the main contract types.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se busca trabajo en tu país? (How do people look for work in your country?)
facts: Non-EU citizens usually need a permit that allows them to work. Rules depend on your nationality and situation, so ask the Oficina de Extranjería or an adviser.
The SEPE (Servicio Público de Empleo Estatal) works with the regional employment services. You register as demandante de empleo (job seeker) and renew it on the dates you are given.
A currículum (CV) is short, clear and in Spanish. Many CVs include contact details, studies, experience and languages, and employers may or may not expect a photo.
After the 2021 labour reform, the contrato indefinido (permanent) became the normal contract. Temporary contracts are limited to specific reasons.
A contrato fijo-discontinuo is permanent but for seasonal or intermittent work, for example in tourism or farming.
Always ask for the contract in writing, and check the type, the salary, the working hours and the convenio colectivo (collective agreement) that applies.

topics.title: Spain's languages: castellano and the co-official languages
topics.sourceNote: Based on the Constitution of 1978 (article 3) and the Statutes of Autonomy of the comunidades concerned. Use of languages in school and administration is set by each region, so ask locally (as of 2026).
topics.intro: Spanish (castellano) is the official language of the whole State, and in several comunidades autónomas other languages are co-official with it. This affects schools, public signs and dealings with the administration.
topics.question: ¿Qué idiomas se hablan en tu región? (Which languages are spoken in your region?)
facts: The Constitution says that castellano is the official language of the State and that everyone has the duty to know it and the right to use it.
Other Spanish languages are co-official in their territories, according to the Statutes of Autonomy of each comunidad.
Catalan is co-official in Cataluña and the Islas Baleares. Valencian is the name used in the Comunitat Valenciana, and it is also co-official there.
Gallego is co-official in Galicia, and euskera (Basque) in the País Vasco and in part of Navarra.
Aranés, a variety of Occitan, is spoken in the Val d'Aran in Cataluña, and it is also official there.

Asturian and Aragonese are protected in their regions, but they are not co-official languages. Where there are two official languages, schools, signs and offices may use both, with arrangements that differ by region.

topics.title: Spanish in the world: one language, many varieties
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about where Spanish is official, based on the countries' constitutions as summarised by the Instituto Cervantes and the RAE. Counts differ by method (official, de facto, co-official). Figures change, so treat them as approximate (as of 2026).
topics.intro: Spanish is an official or main language in about twenty countries, mostly in the Americas, and it is spoken by a very large community in the United States too. It is one language with many varieties, and people understand each other.
topics.question: ¿Qué palabras en español conoces de otros países? (Which Spanish words do you know from other countries?)
facts: Spanish is official or the main language in Spain, Equatorial Guinea and most countries in Central and South America. Mexico has no official language at federal level, but Spanish is the national language in practice.

In Puerto Rico, a US territory, Spanish and English are both official. In the United States the Spanish-speaking community is very large, although Spanish is not an official language of the federal government.
In Spain people say vosotros for a group of friends and ustedes for formal address. In Latin America, ustedes is used for both, and vosotros is rare.
In several countries people use voseo, for example vos tenés in Argentina, instead of tú tienes. You will meet both forms.
Vocabulary differs. A car is coche in Spain and carro in several Latin American countries, and a mobile phone is móvil in Spain and celular in many American countries.
These differences do not make some Spanish right and some wrong. The RAE works with the language academies of the other Spanish-speaking countries.

topics.sourceNote: Based on Ley Orgánica 3/2022 on vocational training (boe.es), Real Decreto 889/2022 on foreign university degrees and the pages of the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities and the Ministry of Education, Vocational Training and Sports (as of 2026). Entry rules, fees and waiting times change and differ by region and university, so check the official page before you apply.
topics.intro: Spain has two main routes after school: formación profesional (FP, vocational training) and the university. If you studied abroad, the state can recognise your qualification in three different ways, and it matters which one you ask for.
topics.question: ¿Qué estudios tienes y para qué quieres usarlos en España? (What have you studied and what do you want to use it for in Spain?)
facts: Since the vocational training law of 2022, FP has three cycle levels: Grado Básico, Grado Medio and Grado Superior. They lead to the titles Técnico Básico, Técnico and Técnico Superior.
A Grado Básico cycle lasts two years. Medio and Superior cycles last two or sometimes three years and include practice in a company (formación en empresa).
To enter a Grado Superior you usually need the Bachillerato or a Grado Medio, or you pass an access test. Many people use FP to start work quickly or as a way into university.

University access usually goes through the Bachillerato and the PAU (Prueba de Acceso a la Universidad). Many people still say selectividad, and the exam was called EBAU until 2024. A Grado Superior title can also open the way into a degree.
A university degree (grado) is followed by a máster and a doctorado. Public universities charge a fee per credit, and each region sets the prices, so the cost varies.

Foreign qualifications: homologación lets you work in a regulated profession (for example doctor, architect, teacher), equivalencia certifies the academic level, and convalidación counts subjects towards a Spanish course. University titles go through the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities. School and FP titles go through the Ministry of Education, Vocational Training and Sports. The process can take months, so start early.

topics.title: Leaving a job: preaviso, finiquito and paro
topics.sourceNote: General orientation from the Estatuto de los Trabajadores (boe.es) and the SEPE pages on unemployment benefit (sepe.es), as of 2026. Amounts and deadlines change and your contract or convenio can differ. This is not legal advice: ask a union, a labour lawyer or the SEPE.
topics.intro: When you leave a job in Spain, the way it ends decides what you are owed and whether you can claim unemployment benefit. Read your contract and your convenio (the collective agreement) before you sign anything.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se termina un contrato de trabajo en tu país? (How does an employment contract end in your country?)
facts: If you resign, give the notice period (preaviso) set in your contract or your convenio. Fifteen days is common, but check yours, and hand in a short written letter.

The finiquito is the settlement: it adds up the pay you are still owed, including unused holiday and your share of the extra payments. Read it before you sign. You may write “no conforme” if you disagree.

Dismissal comes in different kinds. As orientation, an objective dismissal (for example for economic reasons) usually brings 20 days of pay per year worked, up to 12 months. An unfair dismissal (despido improcedente) usually brings 33 days per year, up to 24 months.
A disciplinary dismissal for serious misconduct, if the court finds it fair, brings no compensation. The employer must give you a dismissal letter (carta de despido) that states the reasons.
Paro (unemployment benefit) usually needs at least 360 days of contributions in the last six years and an involuntary loss of the job. A normal voluntary resignation gives no paro.

To challenge a dismissal you have 20 working days. You first file a papeleta de conciliación at the mediation service, and then, if there is no agreement, you go to the labour court. Do not wait: the deadline is strict.

topics.title: Public media: RTVE and regional broadcasters
topics.sourceNote: Based on Ley 8/2009 on the financing of RTVE and Real Decreto 1004/2010 (boe.es) and the public information of RTVE (rtve.es), as of 2026. Funding rules and the board of RTVE are revised from time to time, so check the official pages.
topics.intro: RTVE is Spain's public broadcaster, and it is paid for by the state and by levies on private companies, not by a television licence. In Spain there is no licence fee, and RTVE runs without ordinary adverts.
topics.question: ¿Crees que todos deberíamos pagar una televisión pública? ¿Por qué? (Do you think we should all pay for a public television? Why?)
facts: RTVE (Corporación de Radio y Televisión Española) runs the channels La 1, La 2, 24 Horas and Teledeporte, the radio of RNE, and the streaming platform RTVE Play.
There is no TV licence in Spain. You do not register a television or pay a household fee to watch RTVE.
RTVE is financed mainly by an annual contribution from the state budget, by levies on private television companies and on telecommunications operators, and by a part of the radio spectrum fee.
Since 2010 RTVE has not shown ordinary advertising. The levies on private broadcasters and telecom operators were introduced in the 2009 law to make up for that.
Many regions also have their own public broadcaster. Examples are Telemadrid, Canal Sur, TVG in Galicia, ETB in the Basque Country and 3Cat in Catalonia. Many belong to the association FORTA.
Regional broadcasters are paid by their regional governments. Some broadcast in a co-official language, such as Catalan, Galician or Basque, so they are a good source of listening practice.

How RTVE and the regional channels should be funded and run is discussed in public, and the rules have been changed more than once.

topics.title: Asociaciones, peñas and volunteering
topics.sourceNote: Based on the right of association in Article 22 of the Constitution and Ley Orgánica 1/2002 on the right of association (boe.es), and on the public information of Cruz Roja and Cáritas, as of 2026. Registration steps and volunteer rules differ by region and organisation, so ask the organisation or your town hall.
topics.intro: In Spain, many people join an asociación to meet others, share a hobby or help in their neighbourhood. It is a good way to practise Spanish and to find your place in a new town.
topics.question: ¿Perteneces a alguna asociación o grupo en tu país? (Do you belong to an association or group in your country?)
facts: The right to form associations is protected by the Constitution. The main rules are in Ley Orgánica 1/2002. An association is a non-profit group, and it needs at least three founders.
The founders sign an acta fundacional (founding document) and write the estatutos (rules). The association is then registered in the public register, which is mainly for public information.
Members are called socios. They often pay a small cuota (fee), they vote in the asamblea (general meeting) and they elect the junta directiva (board).

A peña is a group of friends or fans, for example for the fiestas of a town or for a football club. Some are formal associations and some are informal groups with a peña house or a table at the fiesta.

At school, parents can join the AMPA (Asociación de Madres y Padres de Alumnos). In some places it is called AFA (Asociación de Familias de Alumnos). It organises after-school activities and talks to the school.

Volunteering (voluntariado) is organised through groups such as Cruz Roja and Cáritas, food banks and neighbourhood associations. Ask what the tasks are, what training you get and whether you are covered by insurance.

topics.title: Latin American traditions and food
topics.sourceNote: General cultural knowledge, with the UNESCO listing of the Day of the Dead checked on ich.unesco.org (as of 2026). Customs differ by country, region and family, and one name can mean different things in different places, so ask people where they come from.
topics.intro: Latin America is not one culture but about twenty countries, and each tradition belongs to a place. In Spain you will meet people from all of them, so it helps to know which country a festival or a dish comes from.
topics.question: ¿Qué fiesta o comida de tu país quieres presentar a la clase? (Which festival or dish from your country do you want to present to the class?)
facts: Día de Muertos is a Mexican tradition on 1 and 2 November. Families build an ofrenda (an altar) with photos, candles, cempasúchil flowers and pan de muerto. UNESCO lists the Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead in Mexico, since 2008.

The quinceañera is the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday. It is known in Mexico and in many other Latin American countries, with a mass, a dress and a party. How it looks depends on the country and the family.
Inti Raymi, the festival of the sun, is Inca in origin. It is celebrated around the June solstice, most famously in Cuzco in Peru, and it is also held in Andean communities in Ecuador.
The Carnaval de Barranquilla takes place in Colombia, on the Caribbean coast, in the days before Lent. It is known for its parades, costumes, music and dances.
Mate is an infusion drunk from a gourd with a metal straw, the bombilla. It is shared in a group, especially in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay.
Arepas are maize cakes eaten in Venezuela and Colombia, filled with cheese, meat or beans. Tacos are a Mexican dish: a tortilla with a filling. Each country has many regional versions.

topics.title: The State of Autonomies: State, communities, provinces, municipios
topics.sourceNote: Spanish Constitution, Title VIII (art. 137, 143, 148, 149, 151), BOE; municipality count from the INE and the Anuario estadístico of the Ministerio de Agricultura, Pesca y Alimentación, as of 1 January 2025. Which office handles what can differ by community, so check the official page of your town hall or community.
topics.intro: Spain is one State organised into municipios, provinces and 17 comunidades autónomas, and each level has its own tasks. Knowing which level handles what tells you where to go for a school place, a health appointment, a licence or a certificate.
topics.question: ¿Cómo está organizado el territorio en tu país? (How is the territory organised in your country?)
facts: Article 137 of the Constitution organises the State territorially into municipios (municipalities), provinces and comunidades autónomas, and gives all three autonomy to manage their own interests.

Title VIII sets the framework. Article 148 lists what a community may take on, and article 149 lists the matters that belong exclusively to the State, such as foreign affairs, defence and nationality. Each community defines its own powers in its estatuto de autonomía (statute of autonomy).

Communities reached autonomy by different routes. Article 143 was the slower, general route, article 151 the faster one with more powers from the start, and later agreements and reforms narrowed many of the differences. The two autonomous cities, Ceuta and Melilla, have their own statutes.

Spain has 50 provinces. Seven communities consist of a single province, and the Balearic and Canary Islands are organised in islands: consells insulars in the Balearic Islands and cabildos in the Canary Islands. Elsewhere a diputación provincial supports the smaller municipios.
There were 8,132 municipios on 1 January 2025 (INE). Each has an ayuntamiento (town hall) led by an alcalde or alcaldesa. This is the office for the padrón, local taxes, waste and local police.

In practice, health and education are mostly run by the communities, which is why a school calendar, a health card or a public-sector exam can differ between regions. Nationality, immigration law and the Seguridad Social stay with the State.

topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on the public information of the Seguridad Social (seg-social.es), as of 2026. Contribution rates, pension amounts and deadlines change every year and are deliberately left out. Check seg-social.es or ask at a CAISS office before you act.
topics.intro: The Seguridad Social is the public system behind your pension, sick pay and other benefits. You enter it through a personal number and an alta (registration) as a worker. Employees are normally registered by their employer, while self-employed people register themselves.
topics.question: ¿Cómo funciona la protección social en tu país? (How does social protection work in your country?)
facts: You have a personal Seguridad Social number (número de afiliación). It is given once, usually when you start your first job or when you apply for it, and you keep it for life. Keep it with your documents.

For an employee, the employer must give you the alta (register you) with the Tesorería General de la Seguridad Social before you start work. Your vida laboral shows whether this happened. If something is missing, ask the employer and, if needed, the Seguridad Social.

Contributions (cotizaciones) are shared. A percentage is deducted from your gross pay and appears on the payslip, and the employer pays a further share, which is usually the larger part. Exact rates change, so check the official page.
Autónomos (self-employed people) pay their own contribution. Since 2023 the monthly amount depends on your real net income, in income brackets, instead of a single fixed choice.

Pensions are of two kinds. Contributory pensions, such as retirement, depend on how long you have paid in. Non-contributory pensions are for people without enough contributions and with low income, and they have conditions such as residence in Spain.

Your vida laboral is the official record of your periods of contribution. You can request it free of charge from the Seguridad Social, usually online with a digital certificate or Cl@ve, or at an office. Check it from time to time.

topics.title: Elections and the electoral system
topics.sourceNote: Spanish Constitution (art. 68, 69, 99) and the Ley Orgánica del Régimen Electoral General (LOREG), BOE; electoral census and voting rights of foreign residents from the INE and the Oficina del Censo Electoral. Rules for foreign residents depend on bilateral agreements, as of 2023, so check the INE page before an election.
topics.intro: In Spain you vote for parties' lists, not directly for the head of government, and who may vote depends on the type of election and on your nationality. The Congress decides who becomes president of the Government in an investiture vote.
topics.question: ¿Quién puede votar en tu país y en qué elecciones? (Who may vote in your country, and in which elections?)
facts: The Congreso de los Diputados has 350 seats, a number fixed by the electoral law within the 300 to 400 range of the Constitution. Deputies are chosen in 52 constituencies, the 50 provinces plus Ceuta and Melilla, using the D'Hondt method with closed lists.
In each constituency a list needs at least 3% of the valid votes to take part in the distribution of seats. Each province has a minimum of two deputies, and Ceuta and Melilla one each.

The Senado is the territorial chamber. Voters in each province elect senators directly, and the parliaments of the autonomous communities also appoint some senators. General elections are held at most every four years.

You do not elect the president of the Government directly. After an election, the King proposes a candidate after consulting the parties, and the Congreso votes in an investiture (investidura). The candidate needs enough support in that vote.

Municipal elections choose the concejales (councillors) from party lists, and the councillors then choose the alcalde or alcaldesa. Autonomic elections choose each community's parliament, and European elections choose Spain's members of the European Parliament.

Foreign residents can vote in some elections. EU citizens may vote in municipal and European elections, and citizens of some other countries with a reciprocity agreement may vote in municipal elections, usually with extra conditions such as legal residence. Autonomic and general elections need Spanish nationality.

topics.title: Spain and Latin America: a shared history
topics.sourceNote: General historical overview written neutrally. Dates are standard in history reference works; the 12 de octubre holiday follows Ley 18/1987 (BOE). The names used in other countries are from public sources, as of 2026. Historians and governments assess these events differently, and this page does not take a side.
topics.intro: Spain and Latin America share a language and more than five centuries of history, with contacts that went in both directions and that people still judge differently today. Knowing the main dates helps you follow conversations about the 12 de octubre and about migration.
topics.question: ¿Qué fecha de la historia de tu país se recuerda de forma distinta en otros países? (Which date in your country's history is remembered differently in other countries?)
facts: In 1492 two events happened in Spain's history. In January the Kingdom of Granada ended, and on 12 October Columbus's expedition reached the Caribbean. The Spanish Crown then conquered and colonised large parts of the Americas and ruled them for centuries, with devastating consequences for many Indigenous peoples through war, forced labour and disease.

Between about 1810 and 1825 most of the mainland territories became independent in separate processes, including those of Mexico, Gran Colombia, Peru, Argentina and Chile. Deputies from the Americas took part in drafting the Constitution of Cádiz of 1812.
In 1898 Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines after the war with the United States. In Spain this is called the Desastre del 98.

After the Civil War ended in 1939, many Spaniards went into exile. Mexico took in a large group, and other countries such as Argentina, Chile, Venezuela and the Dominican Republic took in others. Spaniards also emigrated to the Americas in earlier centuries.

Since the 1990s the movement has also run towards Spain, with large numbers of people from Latin America settling there. Today people from Latin America are one of the largest groups of foreign-born residents. People from several of these countries can ask for Spanish nationality after two years of legal residence instead of ten, and you should check the current rules.

The 12 de octubre is the Fiesta Nacional de España, set by law in 1987. In several American countries the date has another name and meaning, such as Día de la Resistencia Indígena in Venezuela or Día del Respeto a la Diversidad Cultural in Argentina, and in the United States it is Columbus Day. How to remember the date is debated by historians and politicians.

topics.title: The Transition to democracy
topics.sourceNote: Dates from the BOE, the Congreso de los Diputados and La Moncloa (Ley para la Reforma Política 1976, Ley 46/1977 de Amnistía, Constitución 1978, Ley 20/2022 de Memoria Democrática). How the period should be judged is debated among historians, and this page presents the debate without taking a side.
topics.intro: The Transición was the period after the death of Franco in 1975 in which Spain moved from a dictatorship to a democratic system based on the Constitution of 1978. Historians agree on its main dates and still discuss how it should be judged.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se recuerda en tu país un cambio político importante? (How is an important political change remembered in your country?)
facts: Francisco Franco died on 20 November 1975. Juan Carlos I was proclaimed king two days later.
In 1976 the Cortes approved the Ley para la Reforma Política, which opened the way to elections. It was endorsed in a referendum in December 1976.

The first democratic general elections since 1936 took place on 15 June 1977. The Cortes elected then drafted the Constitution. In October 1977 the Amnesty Law was passed and the Pactos de la Moncloa (political and economic agreements between the main parties and social groups) were signed.
The Constitution was approved in a referendum on 6 December 1978. On 23 February 1981 (the 23-F) an armed attempt to take over the Congreso failed, and the democratic institutions continued.

The Transition is often described as a negotiated, consensus-based process. Others point out that it left open questions, among them the treatment of victims and of those who held responsibility during the dictatorship. These views coexist, and both are part of public debate.
Later laws deal with this memory. A 2007 law began recognising victims, and the Ley de Memoria Democrática of 2022 replaced it. Political groups disagree about its scope.

topics.title: The Constitution of 1978 and the Constitutional Court
topics.sourceNote: Constitución Española (BOE-A-1978-31229), including the reforms of 1992, 2011 and 2024 (art. 49, BOE of 17 February 2024), and the Ley Orgánica 2/1979 del Tribunal Constitucional; tribunalconstitucional.es. Check the current text on boe.es.
topics.intro: The Constitution of 1978 is the highest law of Spain, and the Tribunal Constitucional (Constitutional Court) is the body that makes sure other laws respect it. It was approved by the Cortes and by voters in a referendum, and it sets out the basic rights.
topics.question: ¿Qué derechos garantiza la constitución de tu país? (Which rights does your country's constitution guarantee?)
facts: The Constitution was approved in a referendum on 6 December 1978 and entered into force when it was published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 29 December 1978. It is the basis of the legal system.

Article 1 defines Spain as a social and democratic State governed by the rule of law, states that sovereignty resides in the Spanish people, and sets the parliamentary monarchy as the political form of the State.

Article 2 recognises the unity of the Spanish nation and the right to autonomy of the nationalities and regions. Article 3 says that Castilian is the official language of the State and that other languages are co-official in their communities according to their statutes.

Article 14 says that Spaniards are equal before the law and that nobody may be discriminated against because of birth, race, sex, religion, opinion or any other personal or social condition. Foreigners enjoy public freedoms under the treaties and laws.

The Constitution has been amended three times: in 1992 for the right of EU citizens to stand in municipal elections, in 2011 for budgetary stability (art. 135), and in 2024 to update the wording about persons with disabilities (art. 49).

The Tribunal Constitucional has 12 magistrates, who serve for nine years. It decides on the constitutionality of laws and on the recurso de amparo, which a person can bring after the ordinary courts have decided if a fundamental right has been violated.

topics.title: Unions, convenios colectivos and workers' rights
topics.sourceNote: Constitución Española (art. 28 and 37) and the Estatuto de los Trabajadores (Real Decreto Legislativo 2/2015), BOE; Ministerio de Trabajo y Economía Social. General orientation, not legal advice. Numbers for staff representation depend on the size of the firm, so check the Estatuto or ask a union or the labour inspectorate.
topics.intro: In Spain, the main workplace rights come from the Constitution, the Estatuto de los Trabajadores and the convenio colectivo (collective agreement) for your sector. Unions and elected representatives help to defend them. Joining a union is voluntary, but the convenio usually applies to you either way.
topics.question: ¿Qué papel tienen los sindicatos en tu país? (What role do unions have in your country?)
facts: Article 28 of the Constitution recognises the right to freely join a union and the right to strike. Article 37 recognises the right to collective bargaining between workers' and employers' representatives.

The Estatuto de los Trabajadores is the main labour law. It covers contracts, working time, holidays, dismissal and workers' representation. Your contract and your convenio can improve the minimum, but cannot go below it.

A convenio colectivo is negotiated for a sector, a region or a company. It normally applies to all workers and employers in its scope, whether or not they belong to a union. It sets things like pay categories, working hours and extra leave, so ask which convenio applies to you.

The two largest confederations are Comisiones Obreras (CCOO) and the Unión General de Trabajadores (UGT). Workers choose their representatives in workplace elections, and representation is not limited to members.

Workers elect delegados de personal in smaller firms and a comité de empresa from 50 workers. These bodies receive information from the company, take part in talks about working conditions, and can support you if something is wrong.

A huelga (strike) is legal if it follows the rules. Strike days are normally unpaid, and in essential services minimum services (servicios mínimos) may be required. If you have doubts about your contract or your pay slip, you can ask a union, the labour inspectorate or a lawyer.
